input: Turning now to the question of contingency, it is proposed that the contingency allowance for the upgrade project be set at 6%, and there are strong reasons for holding the figure at this level rather than adopting the lower allowance that has been suggested in some quarters. A lower allowance would effectively price the estimate as though the remaining design work were already complete, which is plainly not the case at this stage. As the cost table in the Costs section makes clear, the quantities for part of the scope still rest on outline design, and it is precisely the items defined least tightly at the outline stage that are most exposed to growth as the design develops. The allowance should therefore be understood as the provision for that growth within the estimate itself, rather than as an optional margin layered on top of it. It is recommended that the steering group hold the allowance at 6% until the design reaches the stage at which quantities are measured rather than estimated. A smaller provision would not reduce the eventual cost of the project; it would merely reduce the share of that cost which the approved figure honestly admits to at this point. The allowance is accordingly tied to the state of the design, and it can properly be revisited when that state changes, as the steering group takes the upgrade project toward FID.
target:
The contingency allowance for the upgrade project is set at 6%, and the figure is held against the lower allowance proposed at the last review. A lower allowance prices the estimate as if the remaining design work were complete. It is not: the quantities in the cost table in the Costs section still rest on outline design for part of the scope, and the items most exposed to growth are the ones the outline stage defines least tightly. The allowance is the provision for that growth inside the estimate, not a margin added to it. The allowance is reviewed against the design state, not against the spend to date, because the exposure it covers sits in the work still to be defined rather than in the work already priced.

The steering group is asked to hold the allowance at its present level until the design reaches the point where quantities are measured rather than estimated. A smaller provision does not reduce the cost of the project; it reduces the share of the eventual cost that the approved figure admits to. Where earlier estimates on comparable work have grown, the growth has concentrated in the same outline-defined items, and the allowance is sized to that pattern rather than spread evenly over the table. The 6% figure is therefore tied to the state of the design, and it falls for reconsideration when the design state changes, at the point the steering group takes the project toward FID.
